title: Lamentations
subtitle: five poems of grief for Jerusalem, set in the alphabet
lead: Lamentations is a small book that does one thing: it mourns. After the Babylonian army broke into Jerusalem in 586 BC, burned the temple and led away the people, someone wrote five poems about it. They are not histories. They are what the survivors could say: that the city sits alone like a widow, that God has acted like an enemy, that mothers cooked their children, that the people had sinned and that it was still too much, and that the LORD's acts of loyal love have not ended and his compassions are new each morning.

Four of the poems are alphabet poems, with the verses or groups of verses running from alef to tav, as if grief could be kept in order by spelling it out from beginning to end. The fifth has the same length and no alphabet. Jews read the whole book each year on the Ninth of Av, and Christians have heard it in the last days of Holy Week. The Hebrew never names the poet. The Plain translates the Hebrew only, in lines that show the shape of the poems.
facts: Hebrew 'Eikhah ("How!", its first word); in the Talmud Qinot, "Laments"; Greek Threnoi; Latin Threni and Lamentationes
Not named in the Hebrew. Jeremiah, by Jewish and Christian tradition; most modern scholars doubt it
After 586 BC; most scholars place chapters 1, 2 and 4 within a few years of the fall and the rest within a generation; a few argue for a later, Persian-period date
Jerusalem and Judah after the Babylonian conquest (the exiles in Babylon are a debated audience)
Five poems: city lament, funeral song and lament psalm; chapters 1-4 are alphabet poems
In the Hebrew Bible, one of the Five Scrolls in the Writings; in Greek, Latin and Protestant Bibles, after Jeremiah (in Greek and Orthodox Bibles after Baruch)

audience.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah after 586 BC: those left in the ruined land, who gathered at the burned temple site to mourn and fast (Jeremiah 41:5; Zechariah 7:3-5; 8:19), and the exiles in Babylon. The poems were not written for outsiders. They were written to be said by a people who had lost their city, their king and their sanctuary.
audience.why: To give grief a form. A people that had been told Zion would never fall, and that God would defend it (Psalm 46; 48; 76), needed words for what had happened, including words that blamed God and words that blamed themselves. The poems let them say both. They also teach the community how to pray when God is the one who has done it: honestly, in order, in the language of covenant, and still to him.
views: The poems were sung at fasts at the ruined temple; Jeremiah 41:5 and Zechariah 7:3-5 show that such mourning went on. This is the most common view, since the poems seem written close to the events.
A smaller group of scholars think the poems were composed or carried among the exiles, who needed to say what happened.

Dobbs-Allsopp and others see in the book the Judean form of a long-lived Near Eastern genre, sung at a destroyed or rebuilding temple, which taught a people how to speak to a god who had let his city fall.
Jeremiah 9:17-20 mentions women whose job was to mourn, and 2 Chronicles 35:25 mentions singers who lamented Josiah. They may have performed the poems; the evidence is suggestive and not firm.

Jews who read the scroll on the Ninth of Av, Christians who heard it in Holy Week, and many other communities that took the poems for their own disasters. Those are later uses, not the first audience.

authorship: Jeremiah wrote it. The Talmud says "Jeremiah wrote his book, the Book of Kings and Lamentations" (Bava Batra 15a). Second Chronicles 35:25 says Jeremiah made a lament for Josiah, kept in "the Laments", and Josephus (Antiquities 10.5.1) says that lament still existed in his day. The Greek and Latin Bibles open the book with a prose preface saying that Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented this lament over Jerusalem. Jerome and the church fathers took it as his.

Hillers, Berlin, Provan, Dobbs-Allsopp and most others deny Jeremiah as the author: the poems differ from Jeremiah in outlook (they mourn the captured king, 4:20; Jeremiah told the people to submit to Babylon), chapter 3's trust differs from Jeremiah's harsher oracles, and the Hebrew text names no one. The poems share Jeremiah's images (weeping, "terror all around", the false prophets), which may come from the same period or from the book's later editing.

Some think the poems are by different poets: chapters 1, 2 and 4 by eyewitnesses, chapter 5 later, and chapter 3 by another hand (Albrektson, Westermann). Others think one poet, or one school, shaped all five (Berlin; Dobbs-Allsopp; Lee on the singers). The poems share an alphabet form, refrains and a movement from third person to first person plural.
A few who date it late
A minority place the poems in the Persian period or later. The consensus keeps them within a generation of 586 BC.
outline: The narrator: the city sits alone as a widow, "no one to comfort her"; the enemy in the sanctuary; the people's hunger
Daughter Zion speaks: "Does this not concern you?", the LORD's winepress, her plea for justice on her enemies
The Lord as enemy: a catalogue of "he has" (swallowed, torn down, cut off), the footstool, festival and Sabbath forgotten, the booth torn down
The poet's tears and the dying children; the false prophets; passers-by clap; a call to cry out in the night
Zion's prayer: "See, LORD, and look: whom have you ever treated like this?"
The strong man: "I am the man", walled in, led into darkness, a bear, a lion, an arrow
The turn: the LORD's acts of loyal love never end, it is good to wait in silence, the yoke, the cheek, God does not afflict from his heart
"We": a call to return and a confession, "you have not forgiven"
The "I" again: tears, the pit, "You came near", "You will repay them"
The gold grows dim: the babies and the jackals, the women who boiled their children, Sodom's end
The sins of prophets and priests; the cry "Keep away, unclean!"; the allies that failed; the LORD's anointed caught in their pits
Edom's cup; Zion's guilt paid in full
The community's prayer: "Remember, LORD"; the inventory of loss
"You, LORD, sit as king forever"; "Bring us back to yourself"; the open ending

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: The siege and fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 39 and 52), Zedekiah's flight and capture, the burning of the temple, the famine, the allies who failed, Edom's part, the survivors at Mizpah and the exiles; when each poem was made and for whom.

lenses.name: Critical scholarship
lenses.desc: Authorship and unity; the Mesopotamian city laments and the weeping city-goddess (Dobbs-Allsopp, Hallo, Kramer, Samet); the personified Daughter Zion (O'Connor, Linafelt); the speakers of chapter 3; the alphabet form; the Qumran scrolls, the Greek and the Latin.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The Ninth of Av and the Five Scrolls; the reading in a low voice; the repeat of 5:21; the kinot; Lamentations Rabbah, the Targum, Rashi and Ibn Ezra; Bava Batra 15a on Jeremiah; post-Holocaust readings.

lenses.name: Christian tradition
lenses.desc: Jerome's Threni; the Office of Tenebrae and its music; the reading of 1:12 as Christ's voice and of chapter 3 as the suffering Christ; the church fathers and Reformation commentators (Calvin); Orthodox and Oriental readings; Jeremiah as a type of Christ; the hymn "Great Is Thy Faithfulness".

lenses.name: Lament and suffering today
lenses.desc: How the book holds guilt and protest together; trauma and memory, survivor testimony, victim-blaming and women's voices (O'Connor, Linafelt, Mandolfo); theodicy and the Joban parallel; how Jews and Christians use the book at funerals and national mourning. This lens takes the place of the usual "Still to come" lens, because the book looks back and its hope (3:21-33; 5:19-22) is a hope in God's character and a prayer for return, not a prophecy of future events.

sections.b: Chapter 1 is the city as a woman: a narrator describes her (1:1-11) and then she speaks (1:12-22). Chapter 2 is about the Lord's own acts of destruction (2:1-10), the poet's tears (2:11-19) and the city's prayer (2:20-22). Chapter 3 is a man's lament that turns in the middle (3:21-39), becomes the community's confession (3:40-47) and ends with a remembered rescue and a prayer for repayment (3:48-66). Chapter 4 compares what the people were with what they became, names the sins of prophets and priests and ends with Edom and Zion (4:21-22). Chapter 5 is a prayer by the whole community. Read in order, the poems move from description ("she sits alone") to direct address of God (chapter 5 speaks to him from beginning to end).

sections.h: The alphabet and the limping measure
sections.b: Chapters 1, 2 and 4 give each verse the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, alef to tav; chapter 3 gives each letter three verses; chapter 5 has 22 verses without the letters. The Plain cannot keep this. It marks the alphabet in notes at 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, 4:1 and 5:1, with a table of all 22 letters on each chapter page, and with letter headings in chapter 3 as it does for Psalm 119. In chapter 1 the letter ayin comes before pe; in chapters 2, 3 and 4 pe comes first. Scholars suggest a second alphabetical order in use, a scribe's switch, or a deliberate break after chapter 1; no view is settled. Why the form? One view is that the whole alphabet, alef to tav, means completeness: saying everything, with order, when everything has fallen apart. Commentators give further reasons; none can be proved. The lines also have a rhythm: a longer line followed by a shorter, the qinah or "limping" measure (Budde; Hillers). The Plain shows it with three short lines to a verse in chapters 1 and 2, one in chapter 3, two in chapters 4 and 5.

sections.h: The title, the author and the Greek and Latin preface
sections.b: The Hebrew title is the first word, 'eikhah, "How!": the cry of a funeral song (2 Samuel 1:19, 25, 27; Isaiah 1:21; Jeremiah 48:17). The Talmud names the book Qinot, "Laments". The Greek calls it Threnoi, Latin Threni or Lamentationes, and the English name comes from the Latin. The Greek Bible and the Latin Bible (in the Clementine Vulgate) both preface chapter 1 with a prose sentence saying that Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented over Jerusalem; the two end differently. The Hebrew has no such preface. See the note at 1:1 for the whole question of authorship.

All five poems were written after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (some scholars date the fall to 587 BC). Most scholars place chapters 1, 2 and 4 within a few years, and 3 and 5 later in the exile's early decades. The Plain uses 586 BC, as in its 2 Kings and Jeremiah. The facts behind the poems are in 2 Kings 25:1-21, 2 Chronicles 36:11-21 and Jeremiah 39 and 52: the siege, the breach, the king caught on the plains of Jericho and blinded, the burning of the temple, the deportation, the governor Gedaliah and the survivors at Mizpah (Jeremiah 40-41). Lamentations does not name a king, a general, a date or a place beyond Zion, Jerusalem, Judah, Edom, Uz, Egypt and Assyria.

sections.h: A city lament, a funeral song and a lament psalm
sections.b: Three kinds of poem meet in the book. The funeral song (qinah) opens with "How!" and mourns the dead (2 Samuel 1:17-27). The lament psalm brings a complaint to God, confesses or protests, and asks him to act (Psalm 44; 74; 79). Westermann read chapter 3 as a lament of the individual. The city lament is an old Mesopotamian family of songs mourning a ruined city, in which the city is a mourning woman (the Lament over the Destruction of Ur and others). Dobbs-Allsopp has argued that Lamentations belongs to this family; Gunkel, Westermann and Hillers thought the Israelite genres were enough. Lamentations differs from the Mesopotamian laments in naming its own God as the destroyer, in its confession of sin, and in having no scene of return.

sections.h: Sin, suffering and God as enemy
sections.b: The book has two voices about guilt. One says the city sinned and was punished (1:5, 8, 14, 18, 20, 22; 3:39-42; 5:7, 16), as Deuteronomy 28 and Jeremiah 5 had warned, and names the sins of prophets and priests (2:14; 4:13). The other says God acted like an enemy (2:4, 5), a bear and a lion (3:10), without saying that the punishment fits. The poet refuses to give God a verdict he does not state (3:37-39). Scholars differ on how far the poems accept that Jerusalem deserved it: Provan and Albrektson stress the acceptance; Linafelt, O'Connor and Mandolfo stress the protest and the dialogue between voices. The Plain gives both.

sections.h: God as faithful: the center of chapter 3
sections.b: In the middle of the book is a hope: the LORD's acts of loyal love (chasdei YHWH) have not come to an end, his compassions are new each morning, and "your faithfulness is great" (3:22-23). The hope is spoken by a man who has just said God is a bear. It leads to advice on how to wait (3:25-30), to the statement that God does not afflict "from his heart" (3:33) and to a confession (3:40-42). It does not last: chapter 4 returns to the starving children, and chapter 5 ends with a question.

Jews read Lamentations on the Ninth of Av in a low voice in a dim synagogue, and repeat 5:21 after 5:22 so the book does not end on the word "rejected". Christians in the Latin church sang it as the lessons of Tenebrae in Holy Week, naming each Hebrew letter before its verse; the traditional close, "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, return to the LORD your God", is not in the Hebrew. Both traditions also use the book at funerals and times of national mourning. See the topic pages on the Ninth of Av and on lament.

The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex. The Qumran scrolls that preserve parts of the book are 3Q3 (1:10-12; 3:52-62), 4Q111 (1:1-18; 2:5), 5Q6 (4:5-8, 11-22; 5:1-13, 16-18) and 5Q7 (4:17-20). They mostly agree with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling, but 4Q111 differs at 1:7, 1:12, 1:14, 1:16 and 1:17-18. The Greek is a literal translation of the revision type (the type scholars call kaige), with a prose preface at 1:1 and the Hebrew letter names written in Greek letters before the verses. The Latin (Jerome) also prints the letter names and has the preface. The Targum (an Aramaic retelling) and the Peshitta (a Syriac translation) are not used as witnesses here. Spelling variants and Ketiv/Qere readings (1:6; 1:11; 1:18; 2:2; 2:14; 2:19; 3:10; 3:20; 3:25; 3:32; 3:39; 4:3; 4:12; 4:16; 4:17; 4:21; 5:1; 5:3; 5:5; 5:7; 5:21) are listed in one line on each chapter page; variants that change the sense have entries.

In the Hebrew Bible Lamentations is in the Writings, among the Five Scrolls (Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther), each read at a festival or fast. In Greek, Latin and Protestant Bibles it stands after Jeremiah; in Greek and Orthodox Bibles after Baruch. The Letter of Jeremiah is Baruch 6 in the Latin Vulgate and a separate book in some Greek Bibles. The Greek and Latin placement follows the tradition that Jeremiah wrote it.

sections.h: Books later linked to Jeremiah's name
sections.b: Several later books use Jeremiah's name or the same events: Baruch (a deuterocanonical book, Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches), the Letter of Jeremiah, 2 Baruch (the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 told as the Babylonian one), 4 Ezra (chapters 9-10 have a weeping woman who is Zion), and the Paralipomena of Jeremiah (also called 4 Baruch). They are later works. None is a source for the Plain.

spec.title: The poems come closer to God one by one
spec.body: My own observation, which overlaps with Lee's and Berlin's work on the voices: each poem is nearer to direct speech with God than the one before. Chapter 1 speaks of Zion and then lets her speak; chapter 2 speaks of the Lord's acts and then has Zion pray in its last three verses; chapter 3 speaks of God as 'he' for twenty verses and then begins to say 'you'; chapter 4 speaks about the city and only at its end about Edom and Zion; chapter 5 speaks to God from its first word to its last. The book may be read as the slow movement of a people from describing God's deeds to addressing him again, and the open ending would then be an address that is not yet answered. It cannot be proved.

prompts: A drawing sketched onto a scroll in ink and ochre: a tall ruined city gate with fallen stones, and a woman in a dark veil seated alone in front of it, her face turned to the viewer, in the style of an ancient manuscript mixed with cave drawing and modern line art, soft hand-drawn edges, no hard rectangle.

A winding street of low stone houses, empty, with a single oil lamp on the ground and a dry jar tipped over, drawn in rough charcoal lines and washes of red ochre, as if sketched on old parchment, soft torn edges.

The 22 Hebrew letters from alef to tav carved in a long ribbon along an unrolled scroll, each letter with a small drawing beneath it (a widow, a gate, a jar, a bow), in the manner of a cave painting and modern sketch, uneven edges.
A row of fifteen candles on a triangular stand, going out one by one, with the last glowing behind an altar, drawn with soft charcoal and gold ink on a scroll, no sharp frame.
reading: A close reading of the Hebrew with a full treatment of the form.
A literary commentary strong on the voices and the images.
F. W. Dobbs-Allsopp, Weep, O Daughter of Zion
The case that Lamentations belongs to the Near Eastern city-lament genre.
Kathleen O'Connor, Lamentations and the Tears of the World
The book read with trauma, survivors and women's suffering in mind.
A study of the book's open ending and of how Jews and Christians have read it.
A commentary by a scholar who stresses the book's acceptance of God's judgment.

traditions.q: Why does God let Jerusalem fall? Suffering and sin
views: God permits evil and draws good from it, and is never the cause of moral evil (Catechism 311). The Church holds that Christ's cross gives suffering a new meaning (Catechism 1521), and its Holy Week liturgy hears the city's lament as Christ's.

Suffering and death entered through the fall and the misuse of human freedom. God does not will them; he enters them in Christ. Orthodox teachers do not read each sorrow as a punishment for a particular sin.

God is hidden in suffering. Luther's "theology of the cross" says that God is known where he seems absent, in the cross and in affliction, and the believer clings to the word of promise against what is seen.

God's providence governs all things, including the fall of cities. He may leave his own children for a time to temptations and sorrows to chastise them for earlier sins and to humble them (Westminster Confession 5.5); Calvin's lectures on Lamentations read the fall of Jerusalem as the judgment of a faithful God on a covenant people.

The Second London Confession (1689), the confession of the Particular (Calvinist) Baptists, states God's providence in nearly the same words as Westminster (chapter 5); other Baptists stress human responsibility and God's patient love.
